lead: This unit explains how things vibrate and how those vibrations travel as waves. You start with simple harmonic motion, add damping and driving, then derive the wave equation for a string and for sound. The last chapters show how ultrasonic waves are produced by a piezoelectric crystal and used in measurement and industry.
about: Chapter 2.1 builds SHM from a linear restoring force. 2.2 extends it to a twisted wire, 2.3 adds damping and resonance. 2.4 turns oscillation into a travelling wave on a string, and 2.5 uses superposition to form standing waves and to compute energy flow. 2.6 treats sound as a pressure wave and introduces decibels and reverberation. 2.7 produces ultrasound with a piezoelectric crystal, and 2.8 diffracts sound with an acoustic grating and lists ultrasonic applications.

chapters.idea: A restoring force proportional to displacement produces sinusoidal motion with a period set by the system, not by the amplitude.
chapters.depth: Displacement x (m), amplitude A (m), angular frequency ω (rad/s), phase φ (rad); x = A sin(ωt + φ). Velocity v = dx/dt = Aω cos(ωt + φ), acceleration a = -ω²x. Period T = 2π/ω (s), frequency f = 1/T (Hz), ω = 2πf. Reference circle. Spring–mass ω = √(k/m), with k (N/m) and m (kg). Simple pendulum T = 2π√(l/g) for small angles, l (m), g (m/s²). Some syllabi call ω the angular frequency or pulsatance. Keep the small-angle condition.

figure.aria: Two sine curves of different amplitude cross zero at the same times, showing that amplitude does not change the period.

chapters.example: A 0.50 kg mass hangs on a spring of stiffness 50 N/m. Find the angular frequency, period and maximum speed if the amplitude is 2.0 cm. Answer: ω = √(50/0.50) = √100 = 10 rad/s; T = 2π/10 = 0.628 s; vmax = Aω = 0.020 × 10 = 0.20 m/s.
chapters.trap: Taking ω as f, or using degrees in sin(ωt); for a pendulum, applying T = 2π√(l/g) beyond small angles.
chapters.leave: Energy of a wave to 2.5; damping and resonance to 2.3.

chapters.idea: A wire twisted by angle θ supplies a restoring torque τ = -Cθ, so a suspended disc oscillates with T = 2π√(I/C).
chapters.depth: Couple per unit twist C (N m per rad) is the torque needed to twist the wire by one radian. For a wire of length l (m), radius r (m) and rigidity modulus η (Pa), C = πηr⁴/(2l). Moment of inertia I (kg m²) of the disc. Restoring torque τ = -Cθ. T = 2π√(I/C), f = 1/T. Some syllabi call C the torsional stiffness or torsional constant. Only a few universities teach this derivation at this depth; the elasticity formula comes from Unit 1.

figure.aria: A straight line through the origin with negative slope: torque is opposite to twist and proportional to it.

chapters.example: A disc of moment of inertia I = 0.020 kg m² is suspended by a wire whose couple per unit twist is C = 0.080 N m/rad. Find the period. Answer: T = 2π√(0.020/0.080) = 2π√0.25 = 2π × 0.5 = 3.14 s.
chapters.trap: Using the diameter as radius in C = πηr⁴/(2l), or forgetting that C is per radian, not per degree.
chapters.leave: Full elasticity derivation to Unit 1; damping to 2.3.

chapters.idea: Damping drains oscillator energy so amplitude decays; a periodic drive can restore energy and cause large response near resonance.
chapters.depth: Equation m x'' + b x' + k x = 0, with m (kg), b (kg/s), k (N/m). Damping ratio ζ = b/(2√(mk)). Underdamped: x = A e^(-bt/(2m)) cos(ω_d t + φ), ω_d = √(ω₀² - (b/2m)²), ω₀ = √(k/m). Critically damped ζ = 1; overdamped ζ > 1. Forced equation m x'' + b x' + k x = F₀ cos ωt. Steady amplitude A(ω) = (F₀/m)/√((ω₀² - ω²)² + (bω/m)²). Quality factor Q = ω₀/Δω. Resonance frequency ω_r = √(ω₀² - b²/(2m²)) for amplitude; phase lag passes 90° near ω₀. Logarithmic decrement δ = (b/2m)T_d if needed. Some syllabi call this driven oscillation.

figure.aria: Two resonance curves: the lightly damped curve has a tall narrow peak near ω/ω₀ = 1, the heavily damped curve a low broad one.

chapters.example: A 0.20 kg mass on a spring of stiffness 80 N/m has damping constant b = 0.40 kg/s. Find ω₀, ζ and ω_d. Answer: ω₀ = √(80/0.20) = √400 = 20 rad/s; ζ = 0.40/(2√(0.20 × 80)) = 0.40/(2 × 4) = 0.05; b/(2m) = 0.40/0.40 = 1 s⁻¹; ω_d = √(400 - 1) = 19.97 rad/s.
chapters.trap: Using ω_d as the natural frequency, or saying resonance is always exactly at ω₀; also mixing ζ with b.
chapters.leave: Wave energy to 2.5; driven piezoelectric resonance to 2.7.

chapters.idea: A stretched string obeys the wave equation ∂²y/∂x² = (1/v²)∂²y/∂t², and the wave speed is v = √(T/μ).
chapters.depth: Transverse displacement y (m) at position x (m) and time t (s). Linear density μ (kg/m), tension T (N). Derivation from net vertical force on a small element. General solution y = f(x - vt) + g(x + vt). Sinusoidal wave y = A sin(kx - ωt); wave number k = 2π/λ (rad/m), wavelength λ (m), angular frequency ω (rad/s), v = fλ = ω/k. Reflection at a fixed end flips phase; at a free end it does not. Some syllabi write the wave as A sin(ωt - kx); the sign choice only sets the starting phase.

figure.aria: The same sine shape shifted to the right at a later time, showing a wave travelling along the string.

chapters.example: A string 1.5 m long has mass 0.030 kg and tension 120 N. Find the wave speed and the fundamental frequency when fixed at both ends. Answer: μ = 0.030/1.5 = 0.020 kg/m; v = √(120/0.020) = √6000 = 77.5 m/s; λ = 2L = 3.0 m; f = 77.5/3.0 = 25.8 Hz.
chapters.trap: Using the total mass in place of μ, or mixing v = √(T/μ) with v = fλ without converting units.
chapters.leave: Standing waves and energy to 2.5; electromagnetic waves to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: A travelling wave carries energy proportional to A² and ω²; two opposite waves superpose into a standing wave with fixed nodes and antinodes.
chapters.depth: Average power for a string wave P = ½ μ v ω² A² (W); energy per unit length = ½ μ ω² A² (J/m); intensity for a wave in a medium I = ½ ρ v ω² A² (W/m²), with ρ (kg/m³). Standing waves on a string fixed at both ends: λ_n = 2L/n, f_n = n v/(2L), n = 1,2,3,...; nodes at x = 0, λ/2, λ,...; antinodes halfway between. Superposition of y₁ = A sin(kx - ωt) and y₂ = A sin(kx + ωt) gives y = 2A sin(kx) cos(ωt). Only a few universities teach the energy and power derivation at this depth; the standing-wave pattern itself is widely used.

figure.aria: Three standing-wave shapes with one, two and three half-wavelengths fitting the fixed ends.

chapters.example: For the string in 2.4 (μ = 0.020 kg/m, T = 120 N, L = 1.5 m), find the fundamental frequency and the average power of a 100 Hz travelling wave of amplitude 2.0 mm. Answer: v = 77.5 m/s; f1 = 77.5/(2 × 1.5) = 25.8 Hz; ω = 2π × 100 = 628 rad/s; P = ½ × 0.020 × 77.5 × (628)² × (0.002)² = 1.2 W.
chapters.trap: Using amplitude instead of amplitude squared in power, or forgetting the factor ½; calling the fixed ends antinodes.
chapters.prereq: 2.4 wave equation and string wave speed.
chapters.leave: Sound intensity to 2.6; diffraction grating to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: Sound is a longitudinal pressure wave; its intensity level in decibels and the absorption of a room decide what we hear.
chapters.depth: Pressure amplitude P₀ (Pa), density ρ (kg/m³), speed v (m/s); intensity I = P₀²/(2ρv) (W/m²). Speed in air v = √(γRT/M), with γ (dimensionless), R = 8.314 J/(mol K), T (K), M (kg/mol). Sound level L = 10 log₁₀(I/I₀) dB, reference I₀ = 10⁻¹² W/m². Absorption coefficient α (sabins, m²) and Sabine reverberation time T₆₀ = 0.161 V/A, V (m³), A (m² sabins). Echo and reflection. Only a few universities teach acoustics at this depth.

figure.aria: A logarithmic curve from 0 dB at the hearing threshold to 120 dB at the pain threshold.

chapters.example: A hall has volume V = 500 m³ and total absorption A = 50 m² sabins. Find its reverberation time. Also find the sound level of intensity 10⁻⁵ W/m². Answer: T₆₀ = 0.161 × 500/50 = 1.61 s; L = 10 log₁₀(10⁻⁵/10⁻¹²) = 10 log₁₀(10⁷) = 70 dB.
chapters.trap: Using 20 log₁₀ for intensity level (that factor is for pressure or amplitude), or forgetting that A in Sabine's formula is total absorption, not floor area.

chapters.idea: A piezoelectric crystal vibrates mechanically when an alternating voltage is applied; at its thickness resonance it launches ultrasound above 20 kHz.
chapters.depth: Piezoelectric effect: mechanical strain produces charge; inverse piezoelectric effect: applied field produces strain. Quartz or PZT plate with electrodes. Thickness resonance f = v/(2t), v (m/s) longitudinal speed in crystal, t (m) thickness. Driver circuit: radio-frequency oscillator feeds electrodes; crystal cuts at resonance. Ultrasound means f > 20 kHz. Advantages: high frequency, stable, rugged. Only a few universities teach the circuit details; keep the principle and the resonance formula.

figure.aria: Block diagram: an RF oscillator drives electrodes on a quartz plate, which vibrates and sends out an ultrasonic beam.

chapters.example: A quartz plate is 2.0 mm thick. Longitudinal sound speed in quartz is 5.7 × 10³ m/s. Find the fundamental thickness-resonance frequency. Answer: f = 5700/(2 × 0.002) = 5700/0.004 = 1.425 × 10⁶ Hz = 1.43 MHz.
chapters.trap: Using the full thickness as one wavelength instead of half a wavelength; forgetting that the inverse piezoelectric effect is the one used for production.
chapters.leave: Applications to 2.8; detailed crystal structure to materials courses.

chapters.idea: A periodic acoustic grating diffracts sound according to d sin θ = nλ; ultrasound is used for echo ranging, non-destructive testing and cleaning.
chapters.depth: Acoustic grating: parallel plates or slits with spacing d (m); maxima at d sin θ = nλ, n = 0, ±1, ±2,...; λ = v/f. Measurement of speed of sound in a liquid: find θ for a known order and frequency. Applications: SONAR and echo ranging, non-destructive testing (flaw detection), medical imaging, ultrasonic cleaning, welding, drilling, cavitation. Only a few universities teach the grating derivation; applications are wider.

figure.aria: Sound strikes a periodic grating and leaves as zero-order, first-order and second-order beams at increasing angles.

chapters.example: In water (v = 1500 m/s) an acoustic grating has spacing d = 5.0 mm. A 1.0 MHz sound wave is incident. Find the first-order diffraction angle. Answer: λ = 1500/(1.0 × 10⁶) = 1.5 × 10⁻³ m = 1.5 mm; sinθ = λ/d = 1.5/5.0 = 0.30; θ = 17.5°.
chapters.trap: Mixing millimetres and metres in d sin θ = nλ, or using the grating formula for the zero order to find a nonzero angle.
chapters.prereq: 2.6 sound waves; 2.7 ultrasound production; Unit 4 diffraction grating for the light analogy.
chapters.leave: Medical imaging details to other courses; light diffraction to Unit 4.
